headline: Cape May Rips: B-minus by day, A after dark — fluke steady, drum's long gone
subhead: Daylight rips fishing is a grind with warm water pushing stripers nocturnal, but the fluke bite and a rebuilding weakfish pattern in the bay are keeping rods bent.
body_markdown:
If you're grading the Rips this week, I'd call it a B-minus in daylight and an A-minus after the sun goes down. That's not a knock — that's just where we are in late July with water this warm. My father used to say the Rips never lie, they just tell you what time to show up, and right now that clock says dusk to dawn if you want keeper stripers.

Here's the why. Water off Cape May Point and through the Rips has been sitting warm — mid-to-upper 70s inshore, and that kind of heat pushes mature bass into a low-light pattern almost every summer. I saw it with my dad running this water in the '90s, I see it now. Fish that would happily crush a bucktail at noon in May are laid up on structure through the heat of the day and only coming up to feed at first light, last light, or full dark. So we've adjusted — I've had better luck the last two trips running the outer edge of the Rips at 5 AM on the tail of the outgoing, drifting live eels and bunker chunks over the humps in 30 to 45 feet, than I have grinding it at noon on bucktails. The bass are there. They're just not stupid about when they eat.

Fluke, on the other hand, don't care what time it is — they care about moving water, and that's been the more dependable game this week. Best action's been on the last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing, working the inlet structure at Hereford and the deeper edges off the Cape May Canyon approach. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom in 25 to 35 feet, have been putting keeper fluke in the box — nothing giant, mostly 18 to 20 inches with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in, but steady enough that a half-day trip is worth your gas. If the current's really ripping, I'll switch to a heavier head and slow my drift with the motor rather than fight it — that's the difference between five keepers and one.

Now, the drum. I know some of you are still asking, and I've got to be straight with you — the black drum run in Delaware Bay is done. That fishery is a May event around Miah Maull, the Fishing Reef, and up toward the mouth of the Cohansey, and by the time we hit late July those big drum have pushed back offshore and out of the bay entirely. If somebody tells you they're marking drum in the bay right now, they're marking something else. Don't waste a tide looking for them.

What is building nicely, and what I flagged last week as a bite worth watching, is weakfish. We said the warm, calm evenings would rebuild that pattern in the back-bay channels and marsh creeks, and that's exactly what's showing up around Fortescue and the marsh cuts off the main bay channel. Nothing blitz-like yet — this is a numbers-building situation, not a blow-up — but working the channel edges on the dropping tide with bucktail-and-squid-strip combos or 4-inch pearl white soft plastics on a light jighead has been producing solid weaks in the 16 to 20-inch range for guys willing to fish it quiet and slow. Evening bite's been the strongest window, an hour before sunset through dusk, which tracks with how weakfish have always behaved in this bay — they don't like bright sun on slick water.

Bluefish are stacking up hard north of us right now, blitzing on bunker from Belmar into Raritan Bay, and I expect that pattern to keep sliding south along the beach as those bunker pods keep moving. We haven't seen that show up at full strength inside Hereford or along the Cape May beachfront yet, but with bait already staging off Wildwood, I wouldn't be surprised if we get a taste of it by early August. Keep an eye on the birds working close to the beach — that'll tell you before I can.

Offshore, if you've got the boat and the fuel, Washington Canyon has been worth the run. Stable high pressure's held warm blue water tight to the edge and boats are finding improving yellowfin and some bigeye activity out there, which makes Cape May one of the better canyon jump-off points on the whole coast right now. Not my usual beat, but I hear the radio chatter at the dock and it's been good enough that a few of the local boys are running out weekly instead of waiting for a weekend window.

Looking ahead, we're sliding into the first-quarter neap, which is going to soften current through the Rips over the next few days. That's not bad news — it actually widens your fishing window past the peak of the tide for eel and swimbait presentations, since the water won't be ripping through so hard that you're fighting drift the whole time. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last hour of dark into first light at the outer Rips on eels, then swing into Hereford on the tail of the incoming for fluke before the sun gets too high. Two bites, one tide cycle — that's the two-bay game working the way it's supposed to.
